entry.title: New York Governor Kathy Hochul Signs AI Chatbot and Baby Monitor Safety Bills
entry.content:
Links: news.bgov.com | source

New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed two laws aimed at protecting children from risks associated with artificial intelligence and connected devices. One bill prohibits AI-powered chatbots from using "unsafe features" when interacting with minors, such as those that are sexually explicit, encourage self-harm, or mimic human personas. The second law requires internet-connected baby monitors to include security features that prevent unauthorized remote access or listening.

The chatbot regulations, which require age verification and grant the state Attorney General the authority to seek civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, are expected to take effect in the coming months. The baby monitor requirements will be implemented within 90 days. These measures are a key part of Hochul's reelection campaign platform, which emphasizes the regulation of social media and emerging technologies.

entry.title: OpenAI Launches Election War Room for US Midterms

The company is bringing together hundreds of employees to review flagged cases and track potential misuse of its artificial intelligence tools until all votes are counted.

The initiative expands on previous safeguards introduced by the company to combat deepfakes, cyber threats, and AI misuse during elections. By centralizing operations, OpenAI aims to rapidly address emerging security challenges and prevent the spread of deceptive content generated through its platforms during the high-stakes political cycle.

entry.title: University of Kentucky Research Administrator Granted Religious Exemption From AI Use
entry.content:

University of Kentucky research administrator David Durman has become the first humanist to receive a Title VII religious accommodation excusing him from personally using artificial intelligence tools at work. Assisted by the American Humanist Association, Durman argued that offloading cognitive and moral reasoning to AI platforms like ChatGPT and Claude violates his humanist commitment to personal responsibility and human flourishing.

Federal courts recognize humanism as a qualifying belief system, affording adherents protections equivalent to traditional religions under federal law. Durman's case follows a similar exemption secured by a Unitarian Universalist software engineer and arrives amid growing legal and ethical discussions regarding workplace AI mandates and broader societal skepticism toward automated technologies.

entry.title: ICE and HSI Conduct Sweeping Surveillance Operation Targeting Left-Wing Groups
entry.content:
Links: wired.com | hacker news

Court documents from a federal conspiracy prosecution in Minnesota reveal that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) have conducted a sweeping domestic surveillance operation targeting left-wing activists, labor unions, and community response networks. Initiated under National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 and funded through programs like Operation Keyhole, the multi-agency campaign utilized undercover agents, drones, and invasive digital tools typically reserved for counterterrorism and international crime.

Defense attorneys and former law enforcement officials compare the directive to the FBI’s historic COINTELPRO operations, noting the vast scale of data collection involving intercepted encrypted chats, financial records, and commercial data brokers. The filings indicate that the surveillance extended far beyond Minnesota to activists and conferences in cities across the United States as part of a broader federal crackdown on opponents of the administration's immigration policies.

entry.title: Stanford Professors File Copyright Lawsuit Against Anthropic Over Claude Training
entry.content:
Links: stanforddaily.com | source | hacker news

Stanford professors Tobias Wolff and Chang-rae Lee are among a group of authors who opted out of the $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic copyright class-action settlement to file a separate lawsuit, Cruz v. Anthropic. The new complaint alleges that Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated copyrighted works from shadow libraries to train its Claude artificial intelligence models.

While the Bartz ruling previously found that using books to train large language models constituted fair use, it blocked the creation of a permanent central library using pirated files. The plaintiffs in Cruz v. Anthropic are seeking statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, significantly higher than the payout provided under the class-action settlement.

entry.title: Silicon Valley AI Political Factions Divide Over 2026 Midterm Spending Strategy
entry.content:
Links: cnbc.com

Political action committees and super PACs backed by Silicon Valley tech heavyweights have divided into competing factions over regulatory strategy in the 2026 congressional midterms. Groups advocating for rapid AI innovation and uniform federal rules have spent approximately $8 million in general-election races, outspending rival factions pushing for strict safety guardrails and state-level authority, which have deployed roughly $6.9 million according to Federal Election Commission data.

Modeled after cryptocurrency industry spending, initial efforts sought to build a unified political machine, but intense infighting and high-profile clashes—such as a $23 million primary battle in New York—have triggered voter backlash. Consequently, overall spending slowed sharply heading into November, with major backers scaling back their contributions amid mounting reputational risks and public skepticism toward unhindered AI expansion.

entry.title: Missileer Watch Tracks Military Emergency Action Messages on Shortwave Radio
entry.content:
Links: missileer.watch | hacker news

Missileer Watch is an online platform that provides a live shortwave radio feed and historical archive of United States military Emergency Action Messages broadcast over the High Frequency Global Communications System on 11175 kHz. The site makes intercepted tactical broadcasts accessible to the public alongside crowd-corrected transcripts and aircraft tracking data.

Developed by former 321st Missile Squadron combat crew member Daniel Frenkel, the project offers transparency into military communication channels without compromising operational security, as the underlying tactical messages remain heavily encrypted. Operating with minimal tracking and open-source licensing, the platform serves as a resource for radio enthusiasts and researchers monitoring strategic command traffic.

entry.title: Privacy Risks of Sensitive Data in Application Log Files
entry.content:
Links: fireborn.mataroa.blog | discussion

Log files attached to software support requests and bug reports frequently contain unintended sensitive information, including screen text, private messages, account identifiers, and authentication tokens. Because applications often log extensive internal state and user interactions during debugging, diagnostic files can inadvertently expose confidential personal data.

Users are advised to treat diagnostic warnings seriously and avoid blindly sharing unfiltered log archives when reporting bugs. At the same time, software developers bear responsibility for adopting safe defaults—such as keeping diagnostic logging disabled by default—and implementing selective logging to minimize privacy risks.
